subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO DECEMBER 31, 1967
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last I informed the house that at an early date I would make a statement, on motions, concerning this proclamation, and I think it appropriate to make such a statement at this time. When my predecessor, now the Minister of National Health and Welfare, introduced the legislation establishing the trusteeship, a serious situation had developed which affected not only the unions and their members, but the whole shipping industry of the vital international waterways of the St. Lawrence seaway and the great lakes.
In this connection hon. members will recall vividly the disruption that occurred in 1962 and 1963, the investigation by Mr. Justice Norris, and its aftermath. The legislation was passed in October, 1963. As I recall, only four members opposed the motion for second reading, and on third reading there was unanimous consent to passage. In its preamble the legislation draws attention to the emergency situation, to the consequent threat to the economy of Canada and to our international relations, and to the necessity for peace, order and good government on the seaway, in the ports, and on the seacoast of Canada.
It was further stated in the preamble that the democratic processes within a certain maritime transportation union had been undermined, and it was recommended that a trusteeship be established to enable the seamen to assume control of their organizations.
From the outset in October, 1963, the trustees have assiduously pursued this and other objectives in the interests of the seamen and the industry, and their annual reports tabled in parliament record the tasks and projects that they established and the progress made.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Their ultimate objective has been and will continue to be the settlement of the basic causes of the unrest which disrupted shipping, and not merely to deal with the symptoms of such unrest which occur from time to time.
In their reports to parliament the board of trustees characterized the fundamental causes of the disruption of shipping as (1) rivalry among the unions and their inability to cooperate or agree on a method of settlement of their problems; (2) an obvious lack of cohesion or co-operation among the employers; (3) the hiring hall arrangements in the maritime transportation industry.
Associated with this latter problem are questions arising out of the manning of ships, the education, training and certification of seamen, and labour turnover. Although limited in effect, these questions still pose serious difficulties for the industry and must be resolved, preferably during the current year 1967.
I am happy to say that progress has been made toward co-operation among the unions, unity among the employers and toward communication among the unions with each other and with the association of employers. The trustees have proved to be a unifying influence. They notified me, however, during the last week of the year just past that several of their objectives have not been fully realized. In my opinion it would be most unfortunate if, for want of time, the work now well advanced were not completed and was ultimately undone, with resulting further disturbances in the industry.
The question of whether the act should be extended was considered by the government on December 29, and the decision was then
11808	COMMONS
Maritime Transportation Unions Trustees Act reached that it was desirable that the trustees be given a further limited period-and I stress the word "limited"-in which to complete the objectives they have established as beneficial for the unions and for the maritime industry generally. The additional time will afford the trustees an opportunity to phase out their operations in an orderly way. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that hon. members and the public generally will be interested and gratified to know that from a high of 32 the staff of the trustees is now only nine, so it will be seen that during the past months the trustees have made real progress in their efforts to wind up their activities.
I am happy to say that the chairman of the board of trustees, Judge Rene Lippe, and the other two members, Messrs. Charles Millard and Joseph Mackenzie, have agreed to continue to serve during the extended term. As results indicate, so far they have done a good job in the national interest, and I would like to extend to them the thanks of the government and, I am sure, of parliament for their work. I might say in closing that this limited extension of time cannot, as has been feared by some, operate to interfere with the collective bargaining due to take place in the industry later this year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO DECEMBER 31, 1967
speechtext:
The minister has today repeated an announcement which was made in the newspapers a few weeks ago, namely that the period of the maritime trusteeship is to be extended for a further term of one year.
It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that there must have been misunderstanding, laxity and divergence of opinion among the trustees if, after three years, a further period of one year is required during which the unions are to be held under trusteeship. In my opinion, and in the opinion of those who have followed this situation closely, no reforms of any significance have been effected by the trustees with respect to the unions. If this had been the case there would have been no need to extend the trusteeship for a further year.
As a matter of fact there have been marked differences of opinion among the trustees themselves. Parliament has found it very difficult to obtain any information from them; the standing committee on industrial relations endeavoured to do so a year or two ago, but without success.
We were unable to elicit any information from the members of the trustee board as to the conduct of elections and other vital important matters which we felt we had a right to

DEBATES	January 16, 1967
know, and that the Canadian public had a right to know. If they had made any reforms during the three years they have been in existence they would have been glad to give this information to members of parliament in the standing committee on industrial relations.
One of the first things the maritime trustees allowed and gave sanction to was the violation of the constitution in respect to elections. The executive of the S.I.U. is exactly the same now as it was prior to the establishment of the board of trustees, except that Mr. Hal Banks is not there any longer and nothing is being done about him.
There has been no guarantee at all of a reformed union so far as the S.I.U. is concerned. This is borne out by the fact that even the Canadian Labour Congress has not made any move toward further affiliation of the S.I.U. within its membership. Now we shall have another year of trusteeship, and if that year is not any more productive than the past three years then I think it will have been a waste of money, because after that period we shall be back to where we were in 1963.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO DECEMBER 31, 1967
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is some two and a half weeks since the proclamation was issued, and a week since parliament resumed its session. I think the time lapse between those two events and the statement today explains perfectly the background for the action being taken by the government, because it has obviously taken that length of time to draft this statement to attempt to explain the inexplicable.
I believe the minister said the main reason for the extension of the trusteeship was that it would be a unifying influence, and the trustees had notified him that several of their objectives had not been met. Therefore I think the responsibility rests on the shoulders of the minister to explain to the house in detail what these objectives are that have not been met. He did not take the opportunity to do that today; I hope he will at some future time.
In passing I might say that the extension of the trusteeship, which is certainly not acceptable to me, probably could have been prevented had the Canadian Labour Congress, instead of dragging its feet, acted favourably on the application which one of the unions under trusteeship made for reaffiliation with that central labour body. Also in passing, if I could make reference to a brief submitted to the Minister of Labour on November 22, 1966, by the Dominion Marine Association, a body of companies in the shipping industry, we might
January 16, 1967	COMMONS
get some insight into the real reason for the
imposition of another year of trusteeship. At page 3 of their brief the Dominion Marine Association said:
The member companies of D.M.A. consider it would be futile to enter into collective bargaining negotiations with the S.I.U. until the problems arising out of implementation of the code-
That is the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
-are disposed of.
This was a declaration by the Dominion Marine Association that it was not too interested in entering into the collective bargaining processes, regardless of what the law says. I think this truly indicates the reason for the extension of the trusteeship, namely that the government desires that there be some sort of tranquilizing imposition upon the negotiations coming up later this year in the hope that the results of those negotiations will more nearly meet the desires of the D.M.A. and the government, and consequently will mean less to the employees working in the industry.
It is interesting to note that the minister said there were certain matters relating to safety, the manning of ships and the like which were also reasons for the extension of the trusteeship. So far as I am concerned this is a bit of an insult to the Minister of Transport from the Minister of Labour, because there rests within the hands of the Minister of Transport the responsibility by law of dealing with matters of manning and safety at sea, things which he has pushed to one side or dragged his feet on for some months. It is a sad state of affairs when one minister has to drag himself up with the help of another to justify the imposition of the trusteeship.
There is perhaps one good feature now that the damage has been done; that is the same gentlemen who were on the board of trustees will continue in that position. I say this because it would be absolutely chaotic if a new group of trustees had to come along in the midst of everything and start all over again. It is for this reason that there might be something good in the announcement made today.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I should like to ask the minister whether he would be willing to table the correspondence between himself and the members of the board of trustees relating to the extension. I should like him to table both his letter and their response. May I sum up by saying that in listening to the minister's statement I was reminded quite a bit of the material used in a kitchen called saran wrap; because certainly
Maritime Transportation Unions Trustees Act the statement was flimsy, obviously transparent and, like saran wrap, covers up that which is inside which has a malodorous air to it.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS TO DECEMBER 31, 1967
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement of the continuation of the trusteeship for another year must be greeted with a certain disquiet considering the length of time which has gone by since the trusteeship first was set up. I am sure the Canadian public does not wish to see a return to the situation which originally produced the trusteeship. I feel they would hope that the extension is not something which is going to put the matter to sleep for another year, and that at the conclusion of that period the problem will rise again with all its difficulties. One would hope that this additional time will be used to finalize some of the problems which still exist regarding that group of unions and the transport industry on the great lakes and the seaway. We know the government has not yet made up its mind in respect of the extradition of Mr. Banks from the United States and the possible injection of that personality back into the whole issue in the coming year. This is a matter of considerable concern.
One would hope that without any legislation being passed, possibly the unions of this country would set terms which would limit the years in office of some of the persons who manage under the present set-up to gain control of the unions and remain in office too long, with neither the unions nor the government of Canada having any power over them. I trust that the year's extension will be used to the greatest possible benefit in settling this issue.

speechtext:
1.	What is the value of all articles, items, utensils, carvings, etc., of Canadian Indian origin in the possession of the National Museum of Canada?
2.	What has been the increase in value of these possessions over the past ten years?
3.	Is any assessment available of the deterioration of these possessions over the past ten years and, if so, what are the details of that assessment?

January 16, 1967

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of State):
subtopic: INDIAN ARTICLES IN NATIONAL MUSEUM
speechtext:
1.	It is not possible to set a monetary value on the varied items in the anthropological collections of the National Museum of Canada. Basically, value of any object is the price which it would fetch if it were sold in the market. For rare books, prints etc. booksellers and art dealers commonly accept as a standard price the money paid for an identical book or print at the last auction at which one changed hands. But the artifacts in the National Museum are mainly things that were individually made; as such, they have no identical twins by whose prices at auctions a value could be established; and so this method of valuing National Museum collections fails.
A number of the objects in our collections have, of course, been purchased at various dates. But the total of their purchase prices would not amount to the value of our collections, for various reasons, of which the chief is that a list of such prices would be very incomplete because it would contain no account of donations or objects collected in the field. A very large percentage of the museum's artifacts were either given by donors or collected in the field, so that no monetary price has ever been attached to them; and very many which were purchased were acquired at dates whose dollar values bear no relation to those of today.
2.	It is impossible to determine the increase in value of the museum's possessions over the last 10 years.
3.	No assessment is available of the deterioration of the specimens during the last 10 years.
4.	Humidifying equipment has been placed in the ethnology storage areas where there are artifacts and specimens which would otherwise dry out. The equipment which we have is the best that can be provided. This equipment which was installed in July of 1961 consists of 6-4,000 watt immersion heaters blower type humidifiers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose on Friday I was urging the minister to give serious consideration to accepting an amendment to new section 314D. The remarks I made on Friday were along the line that we should not repeat the mistakes of previous legislation but should give the Canadian Transport Commission the power to direct.
I asked the minister why he had used the words "may recommend" in the new section in view of the representations which I had made earlier in the debate on second reading and on at least one occasion in the standing committee. His answer seemed to be that the board and the minister should not interfere with private enterprise, and I think he was referring to the Canadian Pacific Railway. His answer to my mind was not sufficient reason, and it aroused me to such a degree that even though I had made up my mind just to ask him to consider an amendment, relying on his good will in an effort to try to produce a good bill, I have in the interim, with the approval of the official opposition caucus committee, prepared an amendment which I hope the minister will accept.
Before I move the amendment I am going to give the minister a copy of it so that he can follow me more precisely as I speak. The words in my amendment are not as strong as I would like them to be. I would like to see the new section read "shall direct", without any "may" in it at all, but I recognize that this might defeat the very purpose for which I am battling. If you tell a board that they shall

January 16, 1967
Transportation
direct then, the human nature of board members being what it is, they would tend not to make any directions at all. Therefore in my amendment I am proposing in effect that the words "may recommend" be left in the new section and that additional words be added so as to give the new super board some feeling of the desire of this committee that they may, if they wish, make a direction.
The second reason why I have softened down my amendment from what I originally wanted is that I recognize there are consequential effects to using the word "shall," one of them being that it would affect the ways and means of the public treasury. If I used the words "shall direct" I could run into a situation where the Chair would have to rule my amendment out of order on good and legitimate grounds. Therefore I have worded my amendment in such a way as to achieve the most of what we on this side of the chamber would like to see in the new section without interfering in any way, so far as I can see, with the balance of ways and means of the public treasury, and in the hope of securing its acceptance by the minister, without that acceptance infringing upon the arguments he put forward even though his arguments, in the words of one of my colleagues, were specious. If I could get the minister's favourable consideration for this amendment we would feel that he would have gone quite a bit of the way toward meeting the ideas of the opposition without in any way tying his own hands or the hands of the commission.
My amendment is that in the second line of new section 314D (1) there be added after the phrase "may recommend" the words "or direct as it sees fit". I have copies of the amendment in French if anyone wishes them. I have talked about my amendment at some length in order to give the minister a chance to read it over before commenting on it, and possibly he would like one or two other official opposition members to comment on it before he makes a statement. This would also give his officials time to examine it.
The amendment would give the commission the option of making a recommendation or an order. If the railways accept such an order then we would have achieved our purpose. If the railways do not accept such an order, particularly if there would be any resultant loss to them, then of course they can follow the procedure laid down later under subclause (3).
I am thinking of situations in which the commission could be shown by its experts that there were various things it could direct the

railways to do, for example, make one railway use another railway's lines for running rights, make one railway abandon one line and use a line of the other railway between the two, or issue directions related to interconnections, which the bill covers, thus making the railways operate more efficiently and thereby saving money for the directors and for the Canadian National organization. I would hope that all such directions would be made for the purpose of having the railways operate better and more economically.
Those of us who live in western areas that were over-built by the railways know of many examples to which my amendment would be applicable. We know that experts, in the form of royal commissions, have recommended that changes be made. We also know that changes have not been made. Therefore, when we are drafting new legislation can we not put our trust once again in a commission but this time give it a little more impetus in the form of direction from the House of Commons by saying it will have the power to recommend or direct as it sees fit? This would also give the governor in council an indication of what was or was not being done by the railways in carrying out the wishes of the commission.
There is a second argument which carries a great deal of weight. Railway management being what it is, I suspect that many times railway management would like to propose certain things that would improve the efficiency of its operations but if one railway first made a proposal then in dealing with the other railway or railways, as the case may be, it would in effect lose some of its bargaining power in the actual working out of the details. For that reason there may be a reluctance on the part of railway management to put forward proposals, hoping that somebody who is neutral will make those proposals so that management will not lose its bargaining power.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I can think of one or two examples where this has been so. I am referring now to experiences I had in the spring of 1961 when I was attempting to get grain moved through the west coast ports. There is no doubt that railway management experts, terminal operators, the people on the dockside and others involved in the movement of grain all advised the minister of the day that all that could be moved through the western ports was 15 million bushels per month. Yet after the railway officials sat down with each other, after the
January 16, 1967

unions sat down with management and after the civil servants sat down with all these groups, they were able to come up with an answer which guaranteed that the capacity of those ports would not be 15 million bushels a month but rather 21 million bushels a month. The records will show that in one month the figure of 21 million bushels was exceeded and in fact 29 million bushels were handled.
Were I to tell the committee of all the examples of what was being done in the name of competition it would drive many members away from the concept of competition. What I am trying to say is that there is good competition and there is bad competition. If competition takes the form of one train crew on one railway hauling grain cars across the crossing to block the other railway's access to the port, this may be competition of the old-fashioned sort but is not the kind of competition which brings about the maximum movement of grain. When this situation was presented to the railways they readily agreed that they could change authority from day to day and thus keep the lines clear. In respect of the movement of grain on the west coast, once you get railway management to sit down with unions, with private business and with government groups you are able to clear away all these little practices which have grown up over the years in the name of competition with the idea of getting the best for one company.
I should like to remind hon. members that if the railways benefit, certainly the terminal operators benefit and the workers at the docks and at the terminals benefit. Certainly the business groups benefit and I know the people of Canada benefit. If with this amendment we can get around a difficulty in respect of railway management and have a board which will move with some dynamism in reducing obstacles in railway management in western Canada and if as a result of this progressive dynamism we can get a reduction in the cost, then we will not be constantly faced with higher freight rates and demands for greater subsidies.
That is the second reason I think it is advisable in the long run to use the words "may recommend or may direct" in respect of the commission. I know the word "may" is not as strong as some of us would like it to be. Possibly this is because we have had such a long experience of suffering under the type of emergency where so-called private enterprise fails to do the best thing in its own interest and then turns around, blames everybody but
Transportation
itself and asks for abolition of the Crowsnest Pass rates, higher freight rates and so on when the answer lies right within itself to a larger and larger degree.
The third point, which is minor but important, is that now that the tremendous movement of grain across the west has removed all the argument that there is any loss in respect of the Crowsnest Pass rates there is even greater reason to make absolutely sure the railways can take advantage of the tremendously increasing net return which they derive from the doubling of the amount of grain so that each year they will be able to make the necessary changes in management and run their railways. One thing that all private business tends to do, so long as there is a profit, is never to worry about the fact that there are still savings to be made.
In presenting these arguments I believe I express the hope of a good many people that we can run these railways in a more efficient manner, that we can keep freight rates down by good private enterprise management and represent the interests of the public by giving to this board not only the right to recommend to the railways but also the right to direct.
Finally, although I do not know what is going to happen when we vote on the amendment concerning the setting up of the stronger type of committee which we recommend, whether we set up this stronger type of committee or continue with the present standing committees which are so much under the control and direction of the government of the day, I am sure that with this particular amendment parliament will have a little better measuring stick by which to ask questions. Not only this, but under this type of amendment we will be able to ask what recommendations have been made to the railways. We will have the right to ask the transport commission what directions they have given and if they have not produced directions to meet obvious inefficiencies we will then have a right to reconsider what we have done under this bill. Whether we have the stronger committee which has been suggested or the present type of committee, the words "direct" or may direct" give a little more leverage. I strongly recommend the acceptance of this simple and yet flexible type of amendment which will strengthen the bill and give the feeling to the people of Canada that they have a little more say over their own economic affairs.

Mr. Chairman, before anyone else speaks I should like to raise one or

January 16, 1967
Transportation
two points. Fix'st, I believe the hon. gentleman made the point that instead of putting the word "shall" into his amendment he was going to use the word "direct" qualified by "may". He suggested that if he had put in the word "shall" it might have involved the kind of amendment that could be moved only after a message from the crown. I cannot help but think that if the hon. gentleman has doubt in the one case it would be just as great in the other case because the direction, no matter whether it be an obligation imposed by this parliament or permission given to this board, does not empower the commission to lay an extra charge upon the exchequer. I suggest it would be equally so with regard to the competence of a private member to amend.
If that is an objection to the amendment I do not think the hon. gentleman has improved the position by saying "may" instead of "shall". I would think, if there is a disposition to accept the amendment, that it would be less objectionable to have the word "may" than the word "shall". In the first place, I do not know how the commission would be able to know when it should. There would seem to be a logical difficulty there.
The second point I should like to raise is that I do not think I have much objection if the direction involved is a direction to the railways to provide running rights over each other's lines in certain cases where a contingent loss to one or the other of the railways might be involved. However, it certainly would not involve an order to them to divest themselves of their property. If the commission directs a railway company to lease something is the commission going to determine at what price it should lease it? If you direct someone to purchase something is that also a direction to sell and, if so, at what price? It does seem to me that, taking this kind of consideration into account, you would arrive at certain difficulties which I think would have to be met by more explicit legislation indicating how the direction shall be carried out and who shall determine the adequacy of the compensation.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I think it is clear from the next subsection that there would be additional costs of operating a line which could be recovered from the treasury and be treated as losses. That is true when it affects one branch line of a certain type, but what would be the situation in ordering a railway company to abandon a certain line when it did not feel there was any loss? That conceivably could be done under
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
this arrangement, but how do you measure that?
It seems to me there would be a host of problems created by any kind of direction which would involve doing anything more than the bill already provides by the use of the word "recommend". The recommendations would be made not just to the railway companies but also, if they involved any kind of intervention by the government, to the Governor in Council, and if some expenditure was required to make compensation or do something of that kind, it would be open to the Governor in Council to ask parliament to provide the necessary money.
I think the suggestion that the commission is not being given adequate powers to accomplish anything that we really would wish to be accomplished is met by the bill as it is. I cannot help but think that a recommendation made public, as it would have to be, indicating quite clearly that there were advantages and what the advantages were, would be something which no railway company could possibly afford to disregard unless it was a patently foolish recommendation and one that could be demonstrated to be foolish.
In any event, if there was a recommendation which involved action by the government it would be perfectly competent on the part of the government, no matter what view the railway company might take, to accept the recommendation if in its wisdom it felt it should and if it was within its power. The powers given to the Governor in Council are a good deal wider than the powers we are asking to give to the commission, and I think for a very good reason. The advisers of the Governor in Council are here and can be called upon to account for their actions by the representatives of the people, whereas it would be of considerable significance if a body which of necessity was in the correct technical sense irresponsible, by which I mean independent, were given the power to say that a property shall be transferred from one person to another. Under those circumstances we would be saying that essentially arbitrary acts should be carried out. I am not going to reject the suggestion out of hand. speechtext:
The minister is aware of many instances in which there is duplication in this country, lines where both the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. are operating in the same district and where one line could be discontinued and the other used by both railways. This situation has been faced again and again and no action has been taken. Under subsection (1) of 314D I take it that if the commmission directed that there be some rationalization with respect to any two lines the company would be required to carry it out. I agree that the minister would have to make consequential amendments to
Transportation
provide for the manner in which the financial terms would be agreed upon, but that should not be very difficult. However, I think that the words which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is recommending should be inserted after the word "to" rather than after the word "companies", so that it would read:
In the exercise of its duties under section 314C the commission may recommend to, or direct as it sees fit, railway companies the exchange of branch lines between companies by lease, purchase or otherwise-
Wherever it is dealing with rationalization, if the commission finds that the making of recommendations is not sufficient to get adequate action to remove wasteful duplication I think it should have the power to direct the companies in question to carry out the program of rationalization set forth by the commission. I do not think that the financial terms need to be an insurmounable obstacle. The minister could either provide that the two companies negotiate and try to agree on a figure or if that failed the commission itself could set down a figure which would always be subject to appeal. Another alternative would be for the legislation to provide that in the event of failure to reach a mutually satisfactory settlement the matter could be referred to the courts.
We are arguing for the principle and I would hope that when the minister discusses it with his officials he will give serious thought to this matter. Mr. Chairman, I hope you will bear with me a little if I generalize to a certain extent in respect of this particular section. In my opinion this bill is one of the most important to come before the house. It affects not only the present and future of railroading but also air transport, road transport and even water transport. Therefore if one section or one clause impinges on another it becomes difficult to stick strictly to the subject matter of the one section.
I come from a pioneer district. An efficient system of railroad transportation is of the greatest importance and that is the reason I feel what I have to say is relevant to this section. To a certain extent we have become bogged down in semantics. The most important question is whether we are or are not going to streamline transportation across Canada so as to give to the pioneering people who need it most the attention they require and often have not had. When one speaks of rationalization this means, I understand, having a rational excuse to streamline our railroad system. I agree with this view 100 per cent. I believe there are a great many clauses in this bill which will help in that regard. I am afraid, however, that a commission such as we have here may become involved in so many duties that it may not be able to see the bush for the trees. In respect of the streamlining of our railroads it may forget that the main reason railroading was started in this country was to give efficient help to the pioneering people.
I had been in this House of Commons hardly a month when I took up this matter with the then president of Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon. Of course Mr. Gordon's main responsibility was the profit and loss situation at the end of the year. This involves getting down to dollars and cents. Our main function is to see that the peoples' money is not wasted. I contend, however, that if we lose sight of the fact that service to the people is the main purpose of transportation it does not matter whether or not the books balance at the end of the year because in that event we have failed in our duty to supply the very vital link between producer and consumer. In this regard we have failed in northeastern Alberta. So, if you will excuse me, I will direct most of my attention to this particular problem.

If the minister will exercise the same patience toward me that I have exercised toward him within the last few hours, I think we might get to the meat of the subject. Whether or not compensation should be paid is dependent on whether or not a profit or loss is sustained. Therefore I think the question of whether there is a profit or loss is very relevant to a discussion of this section because we should not pay compensation to a railway company if that company has not done its best to make sure that the profit or loss is proper. I am not satisfied with the bookkeeping system which is used in performing this particular function. Although I have mentioned Mr. Donald Gordon, I do not blame him for this. He did make clear, however, that their method of coming to a decision was a matter of 23033

Transportation
bookkeeping. I cannot stress this main basis of my argument too strongly. I should like to refer to a specific point and I do so without attempting to delay the passage of this bill. If a railway does not operate efficiently on the ground, it cannot operate efficiently on paper.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Two railways exist in the area I represent and from time to time it has been indicated that they are operating at a loss. Neither of these railway lines has been completed. Therefore they have never had a chance to operate efficiently, whether at a profit or loss. If these lines were completed and still operated at a loss I would be the first to support subsidization or a change in the set-up. The government and parliament should provide some guide lines to this new commission so its members cannot come back five years from now and say they did not know what we wanted. We should make it abundantly clear what we want, and we do not require the services of a Philadelphia lawyer to point out our desires in this regard.
I am sure we all want our railways to operate in this country at the least possible cost. If two ends of a railway line do not meet, how can the railway operate efficiently? Anyone who knows anything about hauling freight on tracks, wheels or horseback knows it is cheaper to haul something 40 miles than 328 miles. This is particularly true when the cost is being paid by the small farmer, the homesteader or the small businessman.
It has taken nine years for me to get the opportunity to speak in this house on this subject. We have been told from time to time that the government intends to accept the recommendations of the MacPherson report. No later than yesterday the minister himself made such a statement. The MacPherson report is already out of date. It took six or seven years before we got around to discussing or implementing it, and today we are faced with an entirely different situation. If the railway lines to which I have referred were operating at a loss ten years ago that is now ancient history, and if they are operating at a loss today they are doing so because a gap in the lines has not been filled. I venture to suggest that if that gap were filled they would begin immediately to operate at a profit.
I should like to be sure that the minister and the government, as well as this parliament, will adopt a forward view in respect of the whole question of rationalization and abandonment. Let us look to the future to make sure that the pioneers still moving into certain

January 16, 1967
Transportation
areas today will have an efficient railway system at least until the end of the twenty first century. That is the kind of thinking which existed 100 years ago and I do not see why in 1967 we should not adopt the same kind of vision which existed in 1867. The people of those days did not get bogged down in semantics or make excuses for themselves because they did not have legal opinions or commissions to study the situation. A handful of brave men with visions, courage, imagination and energy built the great railway lines across this country which by and large have served us well. In a few notable areas these railway lines have not served the people well, and as an example I refer to the Athabasca area which has been served very badly.
Great steps were taken by the former administration under the present Leader of the Opposition. The Pine Point railway line was built under that administration and from the day the steel reached Hay River the line has made a magnificent profit. No company anywhere in Canada would suggest that that line be abandoned. It was built for a specific purpose. In northern Alberta today there exists the richest vein of salt in the world; yet there is only one small salt well in operation. Table salt for the world could be supplied by this area if there were an efficient transportation system between Saskatoon and Lindbergh. This would eliminate the necessity of hauling salt an extra 323 miles.

I have in my hand a letter dated January 6, 1967, in relation to the abandonment of the line to which I have referred. I use this as an example to prove the principle in respect of which I am discussing this new section. It is suggested that 28 miles of line between Spruce Lake Junction and Frenchman Butte be abandoned. As a result, instead of having a 40-mile gap in this line there would be a 68-mile gap. This line is owned by Canada so I have a double duty to discuss it.
The reason suggested for abandoning this line is that it does not make money. How could it be expected to make money when it is not an efficiently built line? New section 314E will give the commission the power to abandon this line on the basis of the figures to which I referred a few moments ago. It may

be shown that this line has only carried so many tons of freight over this 28 miles. Perhaps no thought will be given to whether or not the very opposite result to that desired will occur following the abandonment of this line. If the gap in this line were filled in perhaps the line would show a profit of thousands of dollars. In addition, the people of this area have for years been promised an efficient railway system. If this commission decides that the line should be completed instead of abandoned, what power will it have to make sure this is done?
We have been talking for about two hours about whether or not an amendment might cause the government to impose a slight, additional burden on the taxpayers. I believe in orderly procedure in putting things through parliament, but I do not believe in withholding the right of certain people to earn a living for 40, 50 or 60 years. In this case I have not had the sense before to stand up and instruct the committee, if that is what I am doing, to tell the commission, the government, Treasury Board and the taxpayers to do something they promised to do but have failed to do to my knowledge for over 40 years.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This new section will give the power to abandon lines, but how in the world can a recommendation be made by the commission to abandon a line which has never been completed and never had the opportunity to operate efficiently and take its place in the orderly development of northeastern Alberta? If that is not relevant under new section 314E, I do not know how or when it will ever be relevant. I know I am not allowed to talk about anything which might result in an additional burden on the taspayer. I could suggest that a certain line is losing money and propose an amendment that would mean that the taxpayer would have to pay, and I would be ruled out of order. But surely it is not out of order to prevent this committee, and through it parliament, giving the commission power to stop the proper use of railroads in our part of the country. I could go on and no doubt would be ruled out of order, to mention the effect of this bill on the trucking industry, the air industry and the shipping industry of Canada. I shall not do that; I shall remain very specific in my remarks.
I hope that when the bill is finally passed the transportation commission will look at the debates and say: This is what the representatives from that part of the country intended. They intended an efficient railroad system and
January 16, 1967

if the railroads are not able to provide it and make money they are willing to subsidize them, change their freight rate structure or encourage co-operation between them and the truckers.
What I want to do here, and I think this is the only opportunity I will have to do it, is make sure that no railway line is abandoned in northeastern Alberta until all sides of the question have been heard. This subject was raised by the hon. member for Meadow Lake. I think it is necessary to repeat what he said because this part of the country has been cynically neglected. The answer with regard to that part of the country is the same as that which applied to Pine Point, namely, that we wish to have provided the transportation facilities necessary for the development of this agricultural area. When they are, wealth will flow back to this country as it has in respect of other sections of our great land.
When I came to this house the first promise I made to the people of Athabasca was that I would find out why this railroad had not been completed. In this connection I should like to read to the committee a letter received from Mr. C. W. Rump, secretary of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. As a matter of information, the intention of the board is to await passage of Bill No. C-231 and such provisions respecting abandonment applications as may be in it when it is passed, and then consider the matter in the lights of such provisions.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a brief word about an aspect of this clause which is of great interest to southwestern Ontario. As the minister knows, for some years there has been concern in southwestern Ontario about the freight rates for shipping goods from our part of Canada to other parts of the country. Rates for shipments to eastern Canada have been based on a mileage basis and therefore lower rates were being paid from places like Toronto and Montreal to the maritimes than from Windsor. The rates for shipments to the west, however, are based on block rates and shippers from southwestern Ontario have not been able to get rates based on the shorter mileage through the United States to western Canada. The geographical situation, while reflected in ratemaking to eastern Canada, has not in the past been equally reflected in rates to western Canada from southwestern Ontario.
This problem has been brought to the attention of various governments of different parties and to various royal commissions on transportation by the southwestern Ontario chambers of commerce and particularly the Windsor, Ontario, chamber of commerce on a number of occasions in the past. I myself have raised this matter in the house both when the previous Conservative government was in office and later after our own Liberal party formed the government. I think it is a departure from the usual practice to raise a matter of this type before knowing exactly what would be the attitude of one's own party. In these circumstances one often finds that members who raise such matters when they were in the opposition do not do so when their party is in government. However, I departed from this practice and brought this matter to the attention of my government in the house. Since that particular occasion I have remained in direct contact with the minister and his department on this important matter.
The freight traffic committee of the Windsor chamber of commerce decided to present a
January 16, 1967

further brief on this problem to the transport committee of the house while it was studying Bill C-231. It suggested that the freight rate problem in southwestern Ontario could be at least partially solved by a certain amendment to the wording of section 325 which is covered by clause 48 of the bill. I might add that I met with the Windsor freight traffic committee in Windsor to discuss the proposed brief with them before they appeared before the transport committee and in fact assisted them in making arrangements for their appearance before this particular committee of the house.
When the bill was reported to the house the transport committee did not recommend the particular changes to clause 48 requested by the Windsor freight traffic group. Since 1963 the Windsor area and southwestern Ontario generally have benefited from an unparalleled period of economic growth and development. I think that the policies of the present government, particularly the designated area program and the auto pact, have had a lot to do with this. The need for certain changes in the legislation governing freight rates would have appeared more significant had these other government policies which I have mentioned not worked as well as they did. However, more equitable treatment for southwestern Ontario with regard to freight rates would certainly be helpful in assuring the continuing economic health of our area. It deserves some improvement in its presently existing freight rate situation.
As the government has apparently not accepted the specific form of amendment to this clause proposed by the Windsor chamber of commerce to the transportation committee, I ask the minister to indicate just how this bill can be of assistance to southwestern Ontario. It may be that the specific amendment sought by the Windsor chamber of commerce would have been better suited to the regulatory approach of the previously existing legislation which the bill before us is designed to replace and therefore does not fit in with the different philosophy of rate-making and transportation policy which underlies the proposed legislation. It may be that the minister and the department feel that the aim of the Windsor chamber of commerce to get more equitable treatment in freight rates for southwestern Ontario shippers is in fact being met in the present bill although in a different manner from that specifically sought by it. If that is so may I ask the minister to indicate specifically how this is being done.

The hon. gentleman was a member of the government which had a bill all but ready to be introduced based on the recommendations of the MacPherson Commission, on which bill, as I stated, I based a good deal of Bill C-120 introduced in 1964,
Transportation
and I think he will remember that the majority of the commissioners found that the railways were carrying grain under the Crowsnest Pass rates at a loss. They recommended that payments be made out of the treasury to the railways in respect of that loss. That loss was to be verified each year and the payments adjusted accordingly.
Considering that now, at the introduction of this bill, so many years have passed, that we have had so many good crops and that so much grain has been moved, I did not feel that the commission's recommendation would commend itself to parliament. We could not accept the assertion of the MacPherson Commission any longer. The railways maintain that in some circumstances in some years there is some loss in carrying grain.
We as the government were not prepared to make such an assumption. As we had to provide the transitional subsidies anyway for a few years it seemed that the best thing to do was to have the whole matter canvassed over three years which should be a good period to ascertain the facts. If in the opinion of the commission, not of the railways but of the commission, there was a loss, then the governor in council could in his wisdom recommend to parliament that the loss be made up in accordance with the recommendations of the MacPherson Commission. We were not prepared to assume there would be loss.

I do not think the controversy over Crowsnest pass rates should come up within such a short interval as three years because those rates were investigated by the Mac-Pherson commission and I assume they were dealt with at some length when this bill was before the standing committee. The bill provides that the rates shall come up for discussion at intervals of three years, which may perpetuate a state of controversy over a matter that should not be considered for a longer period of time.
Ten years ago this summer the problem of wheat, which was the biggest political problem at that time, rested in part on my shoulders. At that time we had a 730 million bushel surplus, with a 500 million bushel crop expected, and a surplus of soft wheat in the province of Ontario. Our exports for 1957-58 amounted to 320 million bushels. I had forecast that we would export 300 million bushels and I recall being laughed at across the country as an inexperienced, new minister who did not understand the grain trade. We all have such experiences. In fact our exports amounted to 320 million bushels. Those days are now long past.
I also recall when I was making an intensive study of the grain trade that I advanced the proposition that the practice of getting unduly alarmed over that trade each year was unsound, and that it should be looked at over a ten-year period. In my studies I noticed the rise and fall in the world demand for wheat,

and that over a ten year period the problem tended to solve itself. That has been our experience from 1957 to 1967.
In 1957 nobody could see exports of wheat exceeding 300 million bushels, yet over the last few years we have talked gaily about exporting 500 million bushels. We have increased our acreage under wheat and our crops are larger. We are not concerned about exporting it in the way that we were concerned ten years ago. The reason I mention these facts is that we are incorporating a clause in this bill which says that within three years the Crowsnest pass rates will come up for review.

Mr. Chairman, before the recess I gave some reasons for my doubts on the necessity for an inquiry by the transport commission into the revenues and costs of the railway companies with regard to the grain movement in general, and the effect of the Crowsnest pass rates upon the revenues of the major railways.
Back in 1957 we shipped 256 million bushels of grain in export trade. At that time the railways claimed that they were losing money on this operation. In the last few years we moved twice that amount of grain but the railways are still saying they are losing money. If that is so, then why do the C.N.R. annual reports show an increased revenue and why do the C.P.R. annual reports show increased profits? The MacPherson commission have completed an exhaustive study of the matter. Since the establishment of the commission, the grain trade has been doubled.

I believe quite sincerely that the establishment of an inquiry into the Crowsnest pass rates should be removed from this bill entirely. It might well be argued that as this rate was established in 1898 it is now outdated. The opposite argument could also be advanced, that because the rate was established in 1898, because of the dieselization, the establishment of the heavy track, the better balance on the track and the larger train movement, the rates should be reduced. This would be quite logical. One only has to look at the pamphlet called The Freight Equipment Catalogue, published by the C.N.R., to see the size of box cars for moving grain that were built at that time. Some of them are still in existence.
At that time the average box car could be loaded with 1300 bushels of grain. This has changed in the last 10 years. Instead of a steel frame box car the railway companies are using a complete steel car moving up to 2000 bushels of grain. Recently we have seen the introduction of a new hopper-type car which will load, carry and unload what is commonly called a continuous stream of grain.
I do not believe that the railways have been modernized to any appreciable degree, and I firmly believe that the recommendations based on the MacPherson commission's report will bring to a halt the process of modernization which has been started in the grain trade.
In this particular clause no reference is made to what should be considered as the total cost of the movement of grain. We considered this question in the committee, where we were told by the railway company that 70 per cent of their costs were variable and that 30 per cent were fixed. These are rough figures only. The bill states that all rates shall be compensatory. In the railway committee we were told that this meant that all rates should cover variable costs. In other words the railways are permitted to set a rate which would amount to 71 per cent of their total costs, and the commission would allow this.
How will the commission judge the costs and the revenues of the railway companies? Will it include all the fixed costs or will it include just the variable costs? Will the railway companies have to prove that the Crownest pass rates are only compensatory? In glancing at this clause it might seem logical to some people that the Crowsnest pass rates should cover the total costs, but it is a well established practice that the volume of trade of a given commodity in a given area shall determine the percentage of the fixed cost so
January 1G, 1967



that the greater the volume of a given commodity that is moved, the greater will be the reduction in the rate, regardless of the mode of transport.
This is why it is necessary to ensure that this clause does not in any way outline what shall be the criteria used by the board of inquiry to be set up by the commission. Will it cover all the costs or will it just set down whether or not the Crowsnest pass rates are compensatory?
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The old bill, No. C-120, which the committee studied two years ago and which was not reintroduced under a different number at this session, purported to provide that the Crowsnest pass rates should be compensatory and that the government would allow the railway an extra $9 on the rates-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-to cover the fixed aspects of the cost of moving grain. This bill leads me to believe that 100 per cent of the cost will be provided, and before the bill passes we shall want a better understanding in this regard.
We firmly believe that, if anything, the rate is outdated and in excess of what it should be. We should like to know what costing was used and on what the criteria are based. We firmly believe that in view of the volume of their business with the grain trade the railways cannot be losing money at the present time.
This commission will do nothing but bring about a slowdown in efficiency in the movement of grain on the part of the railways. It will bring about a slowdown of the modernization process which is just beginning to take place in the matter of railway cars and equipment. A study of the C.N.R. freight catalogue indicates that during the last year many means were tried to speed up and effect economies in the handling of grain.
For example, there was the introduction of what is called the prairie schooner, which is a new type of railway car tried last year for the first tune, I believe with some degree of success. There was also introduced the covered hopper car which brought about what is commonly known in the movement of grain as continuous flow loading and unloading of grain. These plant modernizations are a key factor in the movement of this commodity.
One fault which can be found with fixing a set rate on any given commodity is that the commodity tends to become isolated from the movement of other commodities. It also limits initiative on the part of the railways in the
Transportation
modernization or speeding up of the movement of that commodity. To a certain degree this is exactly what has happened with these Crowsnest pass rates. As a result of the demand for Canadian wheat in our export markets the railways have realized that they are 25 or 50 years behind the times in their port facilities and railway plant generally.
This proposed inquiry will not be looking into the provision of modern plant or port facilities, or what I might term modern railway tracks across the prairies. Some modernization will be effected as a result of this bill in permitting applications to be heard for the abandonment of branch lines which are uneconomical and out of date. But in my opinion this proposed inquiry comes at the wrong time and will be using outdated cost figures.
The trouble with the MacPherson commission is that it was initiated in 1959 and its report came out in 1961 and 1962. In those days the railways were losing money and it was felt that some scheme would have to be devised in order to put the railways in a better financial state. That is what has happened, and today we find the railways flourishing in this new atmosphere of total transportation. This inquiry will be looking into revenues and costs which are six years old, so certainly no benefit will accrue to the western farmers.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, this clause in the bill is the thin end of the wedge in the matter of the Crowsnest pass rates. Certainly the parliamentary secretary has shown in his questioning of the officials of the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. that he has no respect or love for the Crowsnest pass rates, and believes they should be increased. In effect, eventually this is what will happen under the bill; and I am sure that most farmers across the prairies will view it with a great deal of scepticism.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me it was quite a while ago that we were discussing this clause, and perhaps to place in proper context what we are discussing I should read part of the clause:
Not later than three years after the coming into force of this section, the commission shall inquire into the revenues and costs of railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament-
And so on. That passage is to be found on page 41 of the bill. A question I asked earlier today and the answer I received from the minister confirmed my fears that this section proposes a greater problem to the welfare of western Canada than the minister will have us believe by his light-hearted reference to the discussion that would take place in the House of Commons in any subsequent parliament that might be considering this whole matter. As I look at this section of the proposed act, I cannot help but feel that it should be removed, because it is unnecessary. I shall try to place on the record the reasons for my feeling this to be the case. If we go back in the past to the time when the Crowsnest pass rates were initiated and guarantees were made to the western provinces and those who produced grain in those provinces, we cannot but realize that at that time the volume of grain being handled, and even the prospect of grain that would be handled by the railways, was indeed a much smaller percentage than it is today. The volume, in terms of hundreds of thousands of bushels, was much less at that time than it is today and much less than it will be in the foreseeable future.
If we consider our railways systems in Canada today, those of us who come from the grain growing areas do not have to consider them very long to realize that the railways have been very, very slow in bringing in changes in the equipment that they use for the handling of grain, and the whole area in which they assemble their carloads at the various points. We realize that there could be a great improvement in this respect.
One of the reasons for the difficulty in this regard has been the fact that we still have relatively small grain elevators across western Canada. Nevertheless, there has not been that change in the composition of a grain handling

January 16, 1967
Transportation
car that there should have been in the period we have under review at this time. In considering the history of grain handling in western Canada, another matter we should take into consideration is the automation that has taken place in regard to locomotives, locomotive power and the load that a locomotive will now pull.
Also in this connection I think of the elimination of the many stations that has taken place in western Canada, and the encroachment that will take place in the years ahead. If we consider all these things we cannot come to any conclusion but that the cost of carrying a bushel of grain today is much less than it was at the time these rights were given to those who handled grain in western Canada. While at that time they were considered to be guarantees to the farmers and communities of western Canada, today they have to be considered in the context of this bill, which talks so much about competition. Realizing that this particular section of the bill looks only one way, namely to rising costs, we cannot help but feel that it is unjustified in so far as concerns the conditions that have prevailed in the handling and transportation of grain by the railways over the past several years.
In this connection we must consider what the railways have failed to do in regard to those areas in which lines could have operated profitably over the last 20 years in the communities of western and northern Canada. We must also realize the other factors that enter into the cost, not only in regard to the shipment of grain but in regard to the shipment of other commodities, and the effect this has on the slowing down of the development of certain parts of our nation. To introduce a special section in this bill that would have no effect other than to discourage further the search for and utilization of modern handling facilities in the movement of grain seems to be one of those impossibilities that in the year 1967 in the parliament of Canada should not be considered at all.
As I have said, this section uses the words, "'not later than three years after the coming into force of this section." The period is not stated. As I read the section, I gather that one *could refer back to any period of time to figure out what the costs have been. The new section continues:
-the commission shall inquire into the revenues and costs of railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament... and shall report such revenues and costs to the governor in council and "the amount of payments necessary, in the opinion

of the commission, to assist such railway companies to meet the costs of operations in respect of the carriage of grain and grain products after the 31st day of December, 1969, at such level of rates;-

We who come from western Canada do not wish to see a review undertaken every three or five years which would raise the same old divisions which have been raised so many times in the past. I think that it ill-becomes a minister of the government representing one of the historic political parties in this country, which has given lip service to the fact that the Crowsnest pass rates were part of the Magna Carta of western Canada. We do not want to be presented with a clause which would have no other effect than periodically to question the validity of those rates and raise in the minds of people in other parts of this nation the question as to whether the government is indeed subsidizing one section of the country for a particular reason.
I know the minister would like to pass over this matter quickly. He can do so by withdrawing this particular clause because I do not believe it serves any useful purpose. It attacks the very fundamentals of the principle which has been referred to over the years by countless Liberals as the Magna Carta of western Canada. Surely the minister, great Liberal that he is, would not want to attack that principle, coming, as he so often likes to remind us, from the great city of Winnipeg, the gateway to the west. Surely the minister does not wish to be the one to obliterate all the good resolutions of the Liberals before him.
Let us take a look at the advances that have been made not only in transportation but in every other field of endeavour. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport shakes his head. We all know he is opposed to the Crowsnest pass rates. He is against the unity which they have given to this country. This used to be one of the arguments which the Liberal party supported but which they do not support any longer, as is

evidenced by this clause and by the stand taken by the parliamentary secretary.

We can understand his concern in that regard but we cannot understand the Minister of Transport, who apparently thinks that the Crowsnest pass rates will jeopardize the rest of Canada. It was those rates which brought Canadians together and which caused the development of the grain-growing industries in western Canada which has been one of the mainstays of our economy. Hon. gentlemen opposite should know better than anyone else the value to this economy of the grain shipments as reflected in the returns during the last two years while they have been in office. Had it not been for that grain trade the financial position of this government and our trading position in the world at large would have been different from what it is at present.
I plead with the minister to withdraw this clause. I do not think it serves any useful purpose. Surely we should not write into the bill a clause setting down that three years from now the whole question should be reopened, and asking the railways to pattern their affairs in the next three years in such a way as to enable them to make a claim on the government of Canada with regard to the handling of grain, and then enabling them to set rates in accordance with the decisions that are made in that regard.

After reading the section, nobody will know whether the rates are compensatory, whether the rates to be paid to the railways will take into account the operation of the railways, the capitalization of a particular branch, the over-all operation of the entire system, or whether the rates apply to certain portions of operations.
Nobody argues that certain portions of railway operations will not pay for themselves. That is what we have discussed for the last two weeks-for the last two years for that matter. Nobody denies that certain railway operations do not pay for themselves.
I remind the minister that the Crowsnest pass agreement was the Magna Carta that built up the west and built up Canada. It tied to us that part of Canada which might have gone to the United States. The railway bound us together, and let us not forget this. Let not the parliamentary secretary grin, as though he

knows it all. Sooner or later all this will have to sink in.
Until the last couple of years the railways have continuously been harping, as had the newspapers in all Canada-other than the western newspapers, of course-that grain movement does not pay. Surely the parliamentary secretary must have read that at one time. Today one does not hear that, because grain movement is a paying proposition.
We are suddenly told, "Do not fear, nothing will happen; this is merely an accounting process." It is an accounting process for whom? This is an opening for the railways, who keep harping about the Crowsnest agreement. If they say that the 22 cents or 23 cents they get is not compensating them for grain movement, they forget the other aspects; they forget what was given to them under the original agreement.
Nothing in this bill deals with the original agreement. The minister can stand there and talk until he is blue in the face: He will not convince me or any other farmer that he is doing justice to the western farmer. I do not care if he condemns the hon. member for Rosthern, the hon. member for Acadia, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, or any other hon. member for suggesting that this is not the right approach. The minister knows full well that he has opened the whole question.

speechtext:
The minister can stand there and say that it is perfectly all right to charge the farmers more, but that it is not perfectly all right to see what he can get out of the Canadian Pacific, for example. He does not mention that. While I might be one of those who might defend the Canadian Pacific, I am not prepared to accept the notion that we should expect our farmers to move their grain for 50, 60 or 70 miles to the elevator, to prove that the railways can make money.
[DOT] (9:50 pjn.)
You could bring grain to Winnipeg from every point 400 miles or 450 miles away. The farmers, having paid the additional cost, might well move it to the lakehead. But what have you done to the Crowsnest pass agreement? There are several ways of destroying that agreement. One of them is the way the minister is using tonight. He has opened it up. He wants it to be proven to the public-and public opinion can bring a lot of pressure to bear. I know there are more people in eastern Canada than in the west. But if the minister

remembers his words, what he said tonight was that the bulk of the payment for any freight would have to come from the west, anyway, so why would we complain. That is what he said, exactly. It does not matter whether you pay it one way or another: You will have to pay it. That is what he said.
Are we to allow any legislation to erode the Crowsnest pass agreement, or are we not? I cannot stand here and accept what the minister tells us. I cannot for one minute think that the Crowsnest pass must make the grain pay for everything in the west, and then move in other freight over and above-minerals, or lumber or anything else.
I cannot accept the fact that the minister tells us this is nothing, that this is merely an investigation. It is an investigation into what? It is opening a way for the railways to try to prove something to the commission. Whether they postpone this thing for two or three years or whether they start immediately after this bill is passed, it does not matter. The fact is that the reporters will continually harp on this one subject, as they did at the time when there was a suggestion that a transport bill would be passed. Nobody in Canada will convince me otherwise, and I think I follow the press as closely as does any other hon. member, including the minister.
I have not seen much reference to the Crowsnest pass agreement in the last couple of years. One of the reasons is the movement of grain, perhaps a realization that the movement of grain is compensatory. The second is that newspapermen are not going to harp on something which they know they can harp on later, knowing that this legislation exists. Why should any manufacturer in the east have a charge against his final products, when the revenue can be obtained in another way, -through the Crowsnest pass agreement?
Prove to the world that the Crowsnest pass agreement is wrong. Prove to the world that the British North America Act is all wrong, and let us destroy the whole thing. How silly that argument is. Surely there must be some value in the whole thing. I cannot accept the premise that it is all wrong, though there may be weaknesses in it. I cannot accept the premise that we should give the railway companies these gifts, and when the railway companies are given these gifts, that we should not reveal what has happened to the gifts-what revenues they have derived.
The fact is, one must preserve the Crowsnest pass agreement for the benefit of those farmers who have survived because of

it. I am not far removed from a municipality whose potential is not yet fully utilized. There is land there which is still being broken up, land which will produce more grain. Yet no account will be taken of this. We do not realize what fertilizer will do for that country. We do not know what another freight rate will do. Will it stunt the growth of that country? We opened up the best land. We went where we thought the best grain could be produced. From that point on, we had to move into other areas. As the fertilizer became available, new areas were brought under cultivation.
After the war, when machines became available, they broke up that land, and as we were able to absorb the cost, we did it. But if you alter the Crowsnest pass agreement, if we have to pay the full freight rate and on top of that if everything we ship in must travel at the higher rate and everything we ship out must go at the higher rate, I believe we know where to go. I have heard this before under a Liberal government: Join the United States side. Do not think for one moment that this idea cannot be circulated again, and it might be, unless we are prepared to see that this transport is for east and west, for all Canada. This must be a bill for Canada rather than a bill for certain sections, rather than a bill for certain companies.
