maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-ALLEGED TAMPERING WITH MAIL BY HUDSON'S BAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day by way of a question I raised the matter of the activities of the Hudson's Bay Company in handling or mishandling the mail in a certain instance, and subsequently sent photostat copies of the documents I had in my possession to both the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell). The contents of them were also widely publicized because of the intense interest that exists in the matter.
I realize that the Postmaster General may not yet have had an opportunity to inquire fully into that and other matters which were the subject of R.C.M.P. investigation, and thus may not be in a position this evening to indicate fully what course the government is taking. However, following my question in the house the Hudson's Bay Company issued a statement, presumably in Winnipeg.
Although I inquired, I have not been able to obtain a copy of that statement, but I do have with me the references to it which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, January 13. One of the sentences published by the newspaper relating to the statement was as follows:
The H. B. C. statement said Mr. Howard appears
have based his charges on a single incident at Fort Chippewyan, Alta., in November, 1965, which has long since been resolved to the satisfaction of both the post office and the complainant.
The interesting aspect of that is that at the outset the Hudson's Bay Company admits its culpability. At the outset it admits there was such an instance and passes it off as being of no consequence because it happened some

January 16, 1967
11872	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion time ago. It also passes it off as being of no consequence because, as the statement says, the matter had been resolved to the satisfaction of both the post office and the complainant.
Section 55 of the Post Office Act is singularly clear about holding up the mail or unlawfully opening mail. It states that such a practice is an indictable offence, carrying a penalty of $3,000 or three years imprisonment, or both, if the person involved is found guilty. It seems a strange sort of reasoning for the company to say that because the dispute over the payment of an account that Mr. Martin owed the Hudson's Bay Company had been resolved, this wiped out the responsibility of the company, or its liability to a charge under the Post Office Act for having unlawfully opened his mail. No other two people in society can agree, if one commits a criminal offence, that because they resolve their differences there is no longer an offence. I submit it is fairly clear (1) that there was an offence and the company admitted it and, (2) that it tries to get around the fact that it is guilty, because the matter has been resolved so far as the store account is concerned.
The statement, as it appeared in the Ottawa Citizen, mentions that this is an isolated instance. Mr. Speaker, it is not an isolated instance. 1 put to you the proposition that some few years ago at La Ronge, Saskatchewan, where there is a Hudson's Bay store, although the post office was not contained in the store, nevertheless there was an arrangement between whoever was the postmaster and the Hudson's Bay Company, whereby people who were recipients of family allowance cheques and other similar government cheques picked up their mail at the Hudson's Bay store, and not in the post office. In this way the Hudson's Bay store could engage in the same sort of practice with the people there, by having them turn over their cheques to the company and in this way interfere in the normal activities of the mail.
In this instance in Cando, Saskatchewan, while it is not a Hudson's Bay Company store which is involved, nevertheless the situation existed that persons had to deposit their post office box keys with the store manager so that he could open the box, take out the mail containing the cheques, and wait for the person receiving them to open the envelope and sign the cheque over to him in payment for a bill. While I say that in this instance it is not a Hudson's Bay store, it is indicative of the fact that this practice is more widespread


than the Hudson's Bay Company people would have us believe.
While I am not at liberty to disclose the names of the individuals involved, I had the opportunity to listen to a tape recording of an interview in which a woman claimed that the Hudson's Bay Company store manager interfered with her mail. At the present time statutory declarations are being obtained in this regard. It is alleged that when the store manager found out about this he went to this woman in the middle of the night and attempted to obtain a statement from her to the effect that he had not opened her mail.
The people who find these things happening to them are very quiet about them. There may be an element of the responsibility in respect of paying the store bill which is involved, and also the fact that the person concerned will have to go back to that same store and have to deal with this particular manager. They do not wish to jeopardize their credit at the store or their opportunity to obtain food and supplies. This may be the reason that over the years people have remained silent about these practices. At this juncture I think we should urge that these persons make a full disclosure of this sort of practice to the Postmaster General, the Solicitor General, the attorney general in the province or to myself, if they so desire. In this way the type of practice which has been widespread in the north to the detriment of the individuals who have to deal with these stores can be brought to light. While the Hudson's Bay Company is the one company which has been singled out, this practice is not confined to them. Also it is not confined to the one isolated instance in Fort Chipewyan in Alberta as the company would have us believe.
I understand that some time this week at Fort Chipewyan there will be a resumption of the court case involving the store manager. The assault charge in this regard was postponed from last fall. It may be that there will be some extremely revealing information disclosed at this court hearing about this type of practice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the provision in our procedure which permits me to raise a matter in which I am deeply interested and which I raised on Friday last. It concerns litigation involving a Canadian citizen, who is a professional engineer, Geoffrey P. Webb, and The Government of India. Their circumstances of this particular case are as follows, and I want to put them on the record for the first time. I have no doubt they will be raised on many occasions in the future until the situation is resolved.
Mr. Webb served in India for two years as a professional engineer on the Kundah hydro electric project, which is financed through the external aid office under the Colombo plan. Plants three and four of the project, the equipment and engineering services, were gifts from Canada to the people of India. At the end of Mr. Webb's service there in September 1965-some 16 months ago-he followed the normal procedure in such cases and turned his automobile over to the State Trading Corporation of India. I assume he turned over other assets as well.
The State Trading Corporation agreed to pay Mr. Webb 14,508 rupees which were to be converted into dollars at the rate existing at that time. This would amount in Canadian dollars to approximately $3,300. In January of 1966, a year ago, a cheque was issued to Mr. Webb for the agreed amount, and then the trouble began. From that point on it seems to me there began a period of stalling tactics on the part of the government of India. Mr. Webb had a cheque but he could not negotiate it as a result of difficulties put in his way, and
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion could not arrange for a dollar draft to be issued for the 14,000 rupees.
Finally in June of 1966 the rupee, as we all know, was devalued from 4.76 to 7.5 in relation to the United States dollar. At that particular point or within a few weeks the government of India was prepared to pay Mr. Webb for his car at the devalued rate. Because he was not paid in the six month period between the issuance of the cheque and the devaluation he stands to lose some $1,200. So far as I am able to determine this occurred through no fault whatsoever of Mr. Webb. He has been advised on several occasions, directly and through the Department of External Affairs, that he will be paid at the devalued rate. Mr. Webb is not willing to accept less than the agreed price for his car.
The whole transaction could have been completed long before this devaluation, and I feel that Mr. Webb is receiving completely unfair treatment from the government of India. I have not had much experience in matters of this kind, but presumably those members here who belong to the legal profession encounter a good deal more of this kind of thing. It seems to me that if relations between our two nations were not as good as they are, and if India was not a nation to which Canada had given generous help on many occasions, this situation might be understood. We often hear of situations in which people run into difficulties, particularly in matters of immigration, with countries behind the iron curtain. Recently this country sent a very large shipment of wheat to help feed millions of people in India who faced starvation. Canadians are serving in India under the World Health Organization, and in many other ways, to assist them with problems of health and in other fields.
I understand many representations have been made in respect of this case through the offices of our high commissioner to India, but to no avail. I am asking our Secretary of State for External Affairs immediately to bring to bear the full weight of the Canadian government in this matter. I ask that minister, through his parliamentary secretary here this evening, to make the strongest possible representations to the government of India to see that this clear case of injustice is righted.
The facts that I have were not only obtained from this man, but I have here everything documented by our consular division. It confirms everything that has been said by myself this evening and what was said by Mr. H874	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Webb in the first place. This man gave dedicated service in the two years he was in India. During that time he contracted a tropical disease and was very ill, but he stayed in India, met his obligations and complied with the regulations with one very minor exception, namely that he was asked to surrender his passport and declined to do so. I do not blame him at all for this; in my opinion he was quite right.
Our high commission in New Delhi say that they do not believe there is anything more they can do. I could quote a very long paragraph in a letter from the head of the consular division in which they suggest reasons why they cannot do anything more. I am not personally prepared to accept those reasons and I know that Mr. Webb is not prepared to do so. I feel we have to see th^t the shabby treatment of this Canadian citizen is rectified, and what I am asking now is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs deal with this matter personally and at the highest level to see that justice is done.
